decks.title: Planning — Part 1: Meaning, Features, Importance and Limitations
goals: Explain the meaning of planning and why it is the primary function of management
Identify the features of planning in business situations
Explain the importance of planning and link it to controlling
Identify the limitations of planning in a case and suggest how to reduce them

slides.heading: Planning
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what planning is, its **features**, why it **matters** and its **limitations**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what planning is, its features, why it matters, its limitations and how to make plans work
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every successful trip, wedding or business launch begins with a plan. In this chapter we study planning as a function of management. Part one explains what planning means, its main features, why businesses cannot do without it, and also its limitations, because a plan can sometimes hold a business back.

slides.heading: What is planning?
slides.body_md: **Planning** is deciding **in advance** what is to be done, how, when and by whom, so that the organisation reaches its goals.

headers: Example: an imagined juice brand in Nashik
rows: Two new sales executives under the sales head

visual.alt: Table of the questions a plan answers: what is to be achieved (sell 2 lakh bottles this summer), how (supply college canteens and gyms), when (March to June) and who (two new sales executives under the sales head)
visual.caption: Planning decides these in advance.

slides.narration: Planning means deciding in advance. Look at this imagined juice brand. Before summer starts, it decides what to achieve, how to do it, when, and who will be responsible. Once these answers are written down, everyone in the business knows where it is going and how it plans to get there.

slides.heading: The primary function
slides.body_md: Planning comes **first**: the other functions of management are carried out to fulfil the plan.

nodes.label: Planning: goals and the course of action

visual.alt: Flow showing planning first, followed by organising, staffing, directing and controlling, all carried out to fulfil the plan
visual.caption: Every other function serves the plan

slides.narration: Management has five functions: planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling. Planning comes first. Resources are organised, people are hired and guided, and results are checked, all in order to carry out the plan. That is why planning is called the primary function of management.

slides.heading: Seven features of planning

rows: Every plan exists to reach a goal
Found at every level and in every department
One plan follows another, period after period

visual.alt: Table of seven features of planning: focuses on objectives, primary function, pervasive, continuous, futuristic, involves decision making and is a mental exercise, each with a one-line meaning

slides.narration: Here are seven features. Planning focuses on objectives. It is the primary function. It is pervasive, found at every level. It is continuous, as one plan follows another. It is futuristic, because it looks ahead. It involves decision making, since we choose among alternatives. And it is a mental exercise that needs foresight and judgement.

slides.heading: Quick check: which feature?
slides.body_md: A snack maker studies next festive season's demand before fixing production. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: Look for the clue in the time. Is the manager looking back at the past, or forward to a coming period?

slides.heading: Planning at every level
slides.body_md: Top, middle and lower managers all plan; only the **scope and time span** differ.

rows: Monthly output of each cable type
Which worker runs which machine today

visual.alt: Table of planning at three levels of an imagined cable company: the managing director plans a new factory over three to five years, the production manager plans monthly output, and a shift supervisor plans daily machine assignments
visual.caption: Planning is pervasive: scope differs, the activity does not.

slides.narration: Is planning only for the boss? No. In this imagined cable company, the managing director plans a new factory for the next few years. The production manager plans monthly output. A shift supervisor plans which worker runs which machine today. Each plans, but with a different scope and time span. This is what we mean by pervasive.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: spotting a feature in a case
slides.body_md: Board questions often quote a line and ask for the feature.
bullets: Step 1 — Find the clue word in the line
Step 2 — Match it to one feature only
Step 3 — Name the feature and explain it in one sentence using the case

rows: "…studied demand expected in the next festive season…"
"…compared three ways and picked the cheapest safe one…"
"…as soon as the summer plan ended, work began on the winter plan…"

visual.alt: Worked example table matching three lines from an imagined case to features of planning: studying next season demand shows futuristic, comparing and picking shows decision making, and starting the winter plan when the summer plan ends shows continuous

slides.narration: Let us practise. Studying demand for the next season is about the future, so the feature is futuristic. Comparing three ways and picking one shows decision making. Starting the winter plan as soon as the summer plan ends shows that planning is continuous. Always name the feature, then explain it using words from the case.

slides.heading: Why plan? Six points of importance

headers: What it does for the firm
rows: Everyone knows the goal and their part in it
The search for options sparks new thinking

visual.alt: Table of six points of importance of planning: provides direction, reduces risks of uncertainty, reduces overlapping and waste, promotes innovative ideas, facilitates decision making, and establishes standards for controlling

slides.narration: Why do businesses plan? Planning gives direction, so everyone knows the goal. It reduces the risks of uncertainty by preparing for change. It reduces overlapping and waste by coordinating departments. It encourages new ideas. It helps decision making by giving criteria. And it sets the standards that are later used for controlling.

slides.heading: Planning makes controlling possible
slides.body_md: Targets fixed in the plan are the **yardstick**; controlling compares actual results with them.

visual.caption: Imagined figures. Planned targets are the standards; the gap is what controlling acts on.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined paint company. The grey bars are sales targets from the plan; the coloured bars are actual sales. North beat its target by four lakh rupees, West fell short by eight, and South met it exactly. Without the planned targets there would be nothing to compare with. So planning provides the standards for controlling.

slides.heading: Quick check: which importance?
slides.body_md: Two hospital departments stopped ordering the same medicines separately after a common plan. Which importance is shown?
slides.narration: Ask yourself what problem disappeared once the departments planned together.

slides.heading: Limitations of planning

rows: Managers feel bound to the fixed plan
May not work in a dynamic environment
Policy, technology or demand changes unexpectedly
Lower levels mainly carry out plans made at the top
Surveys, experts and forecasts are expensive
A plan helps only if it fits conditions and is carried out

visual.alt: Table of six limitations of planning: rigidity, may not work in a dynamic environment, reduces creativity, involves huge costs, time-consuming, and does not guarantee success, each with the reason it arises

slides.narration: Planning also has limits. A fixed plan can make managers rigid. It may fail when the environment changes suddenly. It can reduce creativity, because people below mostly follow orders. It costs money and takes time. And no plan can guarantee success: it helps only if it suits the conditions and is carried out properly.

slides.heading: Rigidity and a changing environment
columns:
**Rigidity**

The plan says Delhi and Jaipur only, so a manager cannot grab a chance in Lucknow.

**Dynamic environment**

A new duty, rule or technology arrives after the plan is fixed, and the plan stops fitting.

nodes.label: Costs no longer match the plan
Plan must be revised or it fails

visual.alt: Flow of an imagined toy importer: the plan is fixed in January, customs duty is raised in March, costs no longer match the plan, and the plan must be revised or it fails
visual.caption: A change in the environment can overtake a plan

slides.narration: Two limitations are often confused. Rigidity is about the firm itself: managers feel bound to the plan even when a better option appears. A dynamic environment is about the outside world: a duty, a rule or a technology changes after the plan is fixed, so the plan no longer fits. In a case, ask whether the problem started inside or outside the firm.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding limitations in a case
slides.body_md: An imagined spice exporter: read each line and name the limitation.
bullets: Step 1 — Underline the costs, delays and refusals in the case
Step 2 — Match each to one limitation
Step 3 — Quote the line as evidence

headers: Line from the case (imagined spice exporter)
rows: "…told the markets were already fixed for the year…"

visual.alt: Worked example table matching four lines from an imagined case to limitations of planning: a large consultancy fee shows huge costs, three months of preparation shows time-consuming, markets already fixed shows rigidity, and staff following instructions shows reduced creativity

slides.narration: This imagined spice exporter paid consultants a large fee, which shows huge costs. Spending three months on the plan shows it is time consuming. A manager told the markets were already fixed shows rigidity. Staff who simply follow instructions show reduced creativity. Name the limitation and quote the line: that is how marks are awarded.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false
slides.body_md: True or false? A carefully prepared plan guarantees success.
slides.narration: Think about everything that can happen after a plan is made.

slides.heading: Making planning work
slides.body_md: The limitations do not mean "do not plan"; they mean **plan wisely**.

nodes.label: Keep plans flexible with review points
Benefits of planning outweigh its limits

visual.alt: Flow of ways to make planning work: keep plans flexible with review points, involve staff from different levels, use follow-up to correct course, so that the benefits outweigh the limitations
visual.caption: Living with the limitations

slides.narration: Do the limitations mean firms should stop planning? Not at all. Good managers keep plans flexible, with review points. They involve people from different levels so ideas are not lost. And they use follow up to correct the plan as conditions change. Handled this way, the benefits of planning are far greater than its costs.

slides.heading: Quick check: a limitation
slides.body_md: Supervisors say, "Top management has decided everything; we just follow." Which limitation is this?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to new ideas from people who only follow orders.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Deciding in advance what to do, how, when and by whom
Objectives, primary, pervasive, continuous, futuristic, decision making, mental
Direction, uncertainty, overlapping, innovation, decisions, control standards
Rigidity, dynamic environment, creativity, costs, time, no guarantee

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of planning, seven features, six points of importance and six limitations

slides.narration: To sum up: planning means deciding in advance what to do, how, when and by whom. It has seven features, from focus on objectives to being a mental exercise. It matters for six reasons, including direction and standards for control. And it has six limitations, such as rigidity and cost, which wise managers reduce with flexible plans.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In case questions, **name the feature, importance or limitation and quote the line** that shows it.
Do not mix up **rigidity** (inside the firm) with **dynamic environment** (outside change).
Pervasive means **all levels**, not "very important".
5-mark answers: five points, each named in bold and explained in one sentence.
slides.narration: Some tips. In case questions, examiners give one mark for naming the concept and one for the supporting line, so do both. Keep rigidity and dynamic environment apart. Remember that pervasive means present at all levels. For five mark answers, write five clearly named points, each explained in a sentence.

decks.title: Planning — Part 2: The Planning Process and Types of Plans
goals: Explain the seven steps of the planning process in order
Apply the planning process to a business situation
Identify objectives, strategy, policy, procedure, method, rule, programme and budget in a case

slides.heading: Planning: process and types
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **seven steps** of planning and the **eight types of plans**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the seven steps of planning, single-use and standing plans, objectives and strategy, policy, procedure, method and rule, and programme and budget
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part two we see how a plan is actually made, step by step, and then the different kinds of plans a business uses. Case questions on this part are very common, so we will practise reading a passage and naming the step or the type of plan.

slides.heading: The planning process

visual.alt: Flow of the seven steps of the planning process from setting objectives to follow-up action
visual.caption: The planning process

slides.narration: Planning follows seven steps. First, set objectives. Second, develop premises, the assumptions about the future. Third, identify alternative courses of action. Fourth, evaluate them. Fifth, select the best one. Sixth, implement the plan. Seventh, follow up to see that it works. Learn the order: questions often ask what comes next.

slides.heading: Steps 1 and 2: objectives and premises
slides.body_md: **Objectives** say what the firm wants. **Premises** are the forecasts the plan is built on.

rows: Demand for school shoes will rise before June
A new GST return rule will start next year

visual.alt: Table of three premises of an imagined shoe maker: demand rising before June affects the production plan, steady leather prices affect the purchase budget, and a new tax return rule affects accounts staffing
visual.caption: Premises are forecasts; all planners should work from the same ones.

slides.narration: The first step is to set clear objectives for the whole firm and each department. The second is to develop premises: assumptions about demand, prices or government rules. This imagined shoe maker assumes demand will rise before June and leather prices will stay steady. If the premises are wrong, the plan built on them goes wrong too.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first step
slides.body_md: Which is the first step in the planning process?
slides.narration: Before forecasting or comparing options, what must a business decide?

slides.heading: Steps 3 to 5: list, weigh, choose
slides.body_md: Identify the options, **evaluate** each on cost, risk and gain, then **select** the best (or a mix).

visual.alt: Table comparing three alternatives of an imagined sweet shop on cost, risk and likely gain: a second outlet is high cost, medium risk and high gain; home delivery is low cost, low risk and medium gain; supplying hotels is medium cost, high risk and medium gain
visual.caption: Steps 3 to 5: list, weigh, choose.

slides.narration: Steps three to five go together. This imagined sweet shop lists three ways to grow. Then it weighs each one on cost, risk and likely gain. Finally it selects the best, which may be a combination, such as home delivery now and a new outlet later. Remember: listing, weighing and choosing are three separate steps.

slides.heading: Steps 6 and 7: implement and follow up
slides.body_md: A plan on paper achieves nothing until it is **put into action** and **monitored**.

visual.alt: Flow of steps six and seven: the selected plan is put into action by assigning people, money and deadlines, then results are monitored and the plan corrected if needed
visual.caption: Steps 6 and 7

slides.narration: In step six the plan is implemented: people, money and deadlines are assigned and work begins. Step seven is follow up. Managers keep checking whether the plan is being carried out and whether results match the objectives, and they correct the plan where needed. Follow up links planning to controlling.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a cloud kitchen plans to grow
slides.body_md: Apply all seven steps to one imagined business.
bullets: Step 1 — Write the objective with a number and a deadline
Step 2 — State at least two premises
Step 3 — Show list, weigh and choose as separate steps
Step 4 — End with implementation and follow-up

headers: What Tiffin Tales (imagined cloud kitchen, Pune) does
rows: Serve 600 orders a day within a year
Office lunches will keep growing; app fees stay the same
More cooks; a second kitchen; a smaller menu
Compares cost, speed and food quality of each
A second kitchen plus a smaller menu
Leases space, hires cooks, sets opening date
Checks daily orders against the target every week

visual.alt: Worked example table applying the seven planning steps to an imagined cloud kitchen in Pune, from the objective of 600 orders a day to weekly follow-up of orders against the target

slides.narration: Here is an imagined cloud kitchen in Pune. Its objective is six hundred orders a day within a year. It assumes office lunches will keep growing. It lists three options, compares them, and chooses a second kitchen with a smaller menu. Then it leases space and hires cooks, and checks daily orders against the target every week.

slides.heading: Quick check: put the steps in order
slides.body_md: Arrange the seven steps of planning in the correct order.
slides.narration: Start with the goal and end with checking the results.

slides.heading: Types of plans

nodes.label: Single-use: one event or project (programme, budget)
Standing: used again and again (policy, procedure, method, rule)

visual.alt: Flow dividing plans into single-use plans for one event or project, such as programmes and budgets, and standing plans used repeatedly, such as policies, procedures, methods and rules
visual.caption: Two families of plans

slides.narration: Plans come in two families. Single use plans are made for one event or project and are not used again, such as a programme or a budget for one occasion. Standing plans are used again and again for situations that keep coming back, such as policies, procedures, methods and rules. Objectives and strategies set the direction for both.

slides.heading: Objectives and strategy
slides.body_md: An **objective** is the end result; a **strategy** is the comprehensive plan to reach long-term goals.

rows: The comprehensive plan to reach long-term goals
Thirty outlets in Telangana in five years
Franchise outlets, local flavours, most funds to the first ten
Where the firm wants to be
Direction, action and resources, given the environment

visual.alt: Table comparing objectives and strategy: an objective is the end result wanted, such as thirty outlets in five years; a strategy is the comprehensive plan covering direction, action and resources, such as franchise outlets with local flavours

slides.narration: Objectives are the end results the firm wants, best stated with a number and a deadline. A strategy is a comprehensive plan. It sets the long term direction, the course of action, and how resources will be allocated, keeping the business environment in view. Here an imagined bakery aims for thirty outlets and chooses franchises with local flavours to get there.

slides.heading: Policy and rule
columns:
**Policy**

A general guide; managers use judgement.

**Rule**

A must or must not; no judgement, usually a penalty.

rows: Specific statement of what to do or not do

visual.alt: Table distinguishing policy and rule: a policy is a general guide that allows discretion and has no penalty; a rule is specific, allows no discretion and usually carries a penalty

slides.narration: A policy is a general guide to decisions, so managers can use judgement, as in we prefer local suppliers where possible. A rule says exactly what must or must not be done, allows no discretion and usually carries a penalty, as in no phones on the packing line. In a case, words like where possible point to a policy.

slides.heading: Quick check: steps in order
slides.body_md: A fixed sequence of steps for a travel claim is which type of plan?
slides.narration: Is it a guide, a strict rule, a way of doing one task, or a series of steps?

slides.heading: Procedure and method
slides.body_md: A **procedure** is the order of steps; a **method** is the way one step is done.

visual.alt: Flow of an imagined procedure for an expense claim: fill in the form, the manager checks it, accounts verifies bills, and payment is made to the account
visual.caption: A procedure: steps in order. A method: how one step is done (for example, scanning bills instead of photocopying)

slides.narration: A procedure lays down steps in order for a routine job, like this expense claim: form, check, verify, pay. A method is narrower. It decides how one task is done, for example scanning bills instead of photocopying them. Both are standing plans, used every time the job comes up.

slides.heading: Programme and budget
slides.body_md: A **programme** sets out tasks, people, time and money for one project; a **budget** states a plan in numbers.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and features
sections.body_md:
**Planning:** deciding beforehand **what** to do, **how**, **when** and **by whom**, so that goals are reached. It is the **first** function of management; organising, staffing, directing and controlling follow it.

**Features**
1. **Focuses on objectives** — plans are made for goals, never for their own sake.
2. **Primary function** — the base for all other functions.
3. **Pervasive** — at top, middle and lower levels, in every department.
4. **Continuous** — when one plan's period ends, another plan begins.
5. **Futuristic** — looks ahead, using forecasts.
6. **Involves decision making** — only arises where alternatives exist.
7. **Mental exercise** — needs foresight, imagination and judgement.

Looking ahead to conditions of a coming period.

sections.heading: 2. Importance of planning
sections.body_md:
1. **Direction:** goals stated beforehand tell staff what to aim at.
2. **Reduces risks of uncertainty:** forecasting lets managers prepare for change.
3. **Reduces overlapping and wasteful activities:** departments act in harmony; duplication is avoided.
4. **Promotes innovative ideas:** the hunt for options brings fresh thinking.
5. **Facilitates decision making:** goals and forecasts give criteria for choosing.
6. **Establishes standards for controlling:** planned targets are the yardsticks for judging results.

**Link to controlling:** planning sets targets; controlling compares actual results with them. Planning without controlling is pointless; controlling without planning is blind.

sections.heading: 3. Limitations of planning
sections.body_md:
1. **Rigidity:** managers feel bound to a fixed plan and cannot seize new chances.
2. **May not work in a dynamic environment:** policy, technology, competition or demand may change after the plan is made.
3. **Reduces creativity:** plans come from the top; lower levels mostly carry them out.
4. **Huge costs:** information, experts and forecasts cost money.
5. **Time-consuming:** long preparation may leave no time for action.
6. **Does not guarantee success:** past success can breed false confidence.

**Reducing them:** flexible plans, review points, participation of staff, follow-up.

sections.heading: 4. The planning process
sections.body_md:
1. **Setting objectives** for the firm and each department.
2. **Developing premises**: forecasts and assumptions; every planner should use the same ones.
3. **Identifying alternative courses of action**.
4. **Evaluating alternative courses**: positives, negatives, cost, risk, returns.
5. **Selecting an alternative** (or a combination).
6. **Implementing the plan**: resources, people and deadlines assigned; action begins.
7. **Follow-up action**: monitoring and correcting.

Tip: steps 3, 4 and 5 are list, weigh, choose.

sections.heading: 5. Single-use and standing plans; objectives and strategy
sections.body_md:
**Single-use plans** serve one non-recurring event or project: **programmes**, **budgets** for one occasion. They lapse when the event is over.

**Standing plans** guide recurring situations again and again: **policies, procedures, methods, rules**.

**Objectives:** end results the organisation seeks; best when measurable and time-bound. All other plans serve them.

**Strategy:** a comprehensive plan that fixes long-term direction, the course of action and the allocation of resources, with the business environment in view.

sections.heading: 6. Policy, procedure, method, rule, programme, budget
sections.body_md:
- **Policy:** a general guide to thinking and decisions; leaves room for judgement (e.g. "promote from within where suitable").
- **Procedure:** a fixed order of steps for a routine activity.
- **Method:** the prescribed way of doing one task or step; the best method saves time and effort.
- **Rule:** a specific do or do not; no discretion; a penalty usually follows a breach.
- **Programme:** a detailed plan of a project: tasks, people, resources and timing.
- **Budget:** expected results in numbers for a future period; also a control device.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing "pervasive means very important": it means **present at all levels**.
- Mixing up **rigidity** (the firm will not change its plan) and **dynamic environment** (the outside world changes).

- 1 mark: the correct option, or the name of the concept.
- Case parts: 1 mark for naming the feature, step or plan, 1 for the quoted line or reason.
- 3 marks: three points, each explained.
- 5 marks: five named points, each explained in a sentence (about 120 words).

questions.stem_md: Why is planning described as the **primary** function of management?

options.text_md: Planning is done only by the owners of a business, never by managers
Organising, staffing, directing and controlling are all carried out within the framework that planning lays down
Planning is the function that takes the least time
Planning is needed only when a business is first started

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Organising, staffing, directing and controlling are all carried out within the framework that planning lays down. Planning comes first: the other functions are performed to carry out the plans it sets. It is done by managers at every level, it is not the quickest function, and it continues throughout the life of a business.

questions.stem_md: Before fixing production for the coming festive season, the manager of *Kurkura Snacks* (an imagined Indore firm) studies expected demand, likely raw-material prices and rivals' launches. Which feature of planning does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Planning is futuristic. The manager looks ahead and forecasts conditions of a future period before deciding: planning is forward-looking (futuristic). Pervasive means it happens at all levels; rigidity is a limitation, not a feature.

questions.stem_md: At *Sahyadri Cables* (imagined), the managing director plans a new factory, the production manager plans monthly output, and a shift supervisor plans which worker operates which machine. This shows that planning is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** pervasive. Planning is carried out at the top, middle and lower levels, each with a different scope: it is pervasive. The other options are true of planning but are not what this situation illustrates.

questions.stem_md: Planning is called a **mental exercise** mainly because it

options.text_md: is done by managers who are trained in psychology
is always written down in a long report
requires foresight, imagination and sound judgement rather than physical work
removes every risk from the future

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** requires foresight, imagination and sound judgement rather than physical work. Thinking ahead, imagining possibilities and judging between them are intellectual activities. Planning does not need psychology training, it need not be a long report, and it cannot remove all risk.

questions.stem_md: Planning is said to **involve decision making** because

options.text_md: all decisions in a firm are taken only once a year
managers do not need to think about alternatives once a plan exists
it requires choosing the most suitable course from among several alternatives
it is concerned only with past performance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** it requires choosing the most suitable course from among several alternatives. Planning is needed only where alternatives exist; the planner evaluates them and chooses one. Decisions are taken throughout the year, alternatives are central to planning, and planning looks to the future.

questions.stem_md: A school-bag maker prepares a plan for the April–June season. As that season ends, it starts preparing the plan for the next season, using what it learnt. Which feature of planning is shown?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Planning is continuous. Each plan covers a period and is followed by a new one: planning is a continuous process. Pervasiveness concerns levels of management; reduced creativity is a limitation.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined hospital in Nagpur, the pharmacy and the surgical ward used to order the same medicines separately, and some stock expired unused. After a common purchase plan was made, this stopped. Which importance of planning is illustrated?

options.text_md: Planning reduces overlapping and wasteful activities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Planning reduces overlapping and wasteful activities. Coordinating the two departments' purchases removed duplicate orders and wasted stock. Reduced creativity is a limitation; the other two are importance points not shown here.

questions.stem_md: The sales head of *Rangoli Paints* (imagined) compares each region's actual sales with the targets set in the annual plan and asks lagging regions for reasons. Which importance of planning makes this possible?

options.text_md: Planning reduces the risks of uncertainty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Planning establishes standards for controlling. The targets in the plan act as standards against which actual results are measured: planning makes controlling possible. The other points are valid importance points but not the one being used here.

questions.stem_md: Halfway through the year, a manager at *Jharna Water Purifiers* (imagined) spots a chance to enter a new city but is told she must stick to the cities and spending fixed in the annual plan. Which limitation of planning does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Planning leads to rigidity. A fixed plan prevents the manager from changing course to use a new opportunity: rigidity. Cost and time are other limitations; success is not the issue here.

questions.stem_md: An imagined toy importer planned its year around low customs duties. Two months later the government raised the duty sharply, and the plan became unworkable. The limitation highlighted is that planning

options.text_md: may not work in a dynamic environment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** may not work in a dynamic environment. The business environment changed in a way the plan could not foresee, so the plan failed: planning may not work in a dynamic environment. Overlapping activities are reduced by planning, not caused by it.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined textile mill, supervisors say, "Top management has already decided everything; we just follow the plan." Which limitation of planning does this reflect?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Planning reduces creativity. When plans are made at the top and lower levels only carry them out, people below have little room to suggest new ideas: planning can reduce creativity.

questions.stem_md: Spending on consultants, market surveys and expert forecasts while preparing a plan points to which limitation of planning?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Planning involves huge costs. Collecting information, forecasting and evaluating options cost money; for some decisions the benefit may not justify it. Pervasiveness is a feature, not a limitation.

questions.stem_md: A firm repeats last year's successful plan without checking whether conditions have changed, and this year it fails. Which limitation of planning is best illustrated?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Planning does not guarantee success. Relying on a plan that worked before creates a false sense of security; a plan helps only if it fits current conditions and is carried out well, so success is not guaranteed. The other options are features or importance points.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Planning is required only at the top level of management.

**Reason (R):** Planning is a pervasive function of management.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: managers at every level plan, though with different scope. R is true: pervasiveness is exactly why A is wrong.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Planning makes controlling possible.

**Reason (R):** The goals fixed during planning serve as the standards against which actual performance is measured.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: without planned targets there would be nothing to compare actual results with.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Planning may reduce creativity in an organisation.

**Reason (R):** Middle and lower-level managers mostly implement plans drawn up by top management and have little freedom to change them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: when people below only carry out fixed plans, their initiative and new ideas get little room.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A carefully prepared plan guarantees the success of a business.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A plan improves the chances of success but cannot ensure it: conditions may change, and the plan must be implemented well.

questions.stem_md: Match each feature of planning with the description that best fits it.

match_right.text_md: Is carried out at every level and in every department
Looks ahead and prepares for events of a coming period
A new plan follows when the period of the earlier one ends

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each feature is described by its defining idea: future orientation, presence at all levels, a never-ending cycle, and intellectual effort.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by planning? Why is it said to be focused on achieving objectives?
questions.solution_md: A definition (deciding in advance) and the link between plans and goals.

answer.model_answer_md: **Planning** means deciding **in advance what to do and how to do it**: setting goals and choosing the way to reach them. It is **focused on objectives** because every plan starts from a goal, and its activities are chosen only because they help the business reach that goal.

questions.stem_md: Explain why planning comes before the other functions of management.
questions.solution_md: Link the other four functions to the plan they serve.

answer.model_answer_md: Planning **sets the goals and the course of action**. Only then can a manager **organise** resources, **staff** positions, **direct** people and **control** results, because each of these is done to carry out the plan. Without a plan the other functions would have no purpose or direction.

marking_scheme.step: Planning sets goals and the course of action

questions.stem_md: *Himsheet Cold Stores* (imagined) in Shimla expects long power cuts during winter storms, so it plans ahead by installing a backup generator and fixing a diesel supply contract. Which importance of planning does this show? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Name the importance point and connect it to the anticipated event and the advance arrangement.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows that planning **reduces the risks of uncertainty**. By **anticipating** a likely future problem (power cuts) and arranging a **generator and fuel** in advance, the firm can keep its stores cold and avoid losses when the event occurs.

questions.stem_md: How does planning encourage new ideas in an organisation?
questions.solution_md: Explain that searching for alternatives produces new ideas.

answer.model_answer_md: While planning, managers must **think of many possible courses** of action and look for **better ways** of reaching goals. This search makes them **creative**: new products, methods and markets are often first proposed during planning, and good ideas then get a place in the final plan.

marking_scheme.step: Leads to new ideas being adopted

questions.stem_md: *Pixelkart* (an imagined online electronics seller) took four months to prepare a detailed plan for a new smartphone range. By the time it was ready, a rival had already launched a similar range. Identify and explain the limitation of planning shown.
questions.solution_md: Name the limitation and connect it to the lost opportunity.

answer.model_answer_md: The limitation is that planning is **time-consuming**. Collecting information, studying alternatives and preparing a detailed plan took so long that the **opportunity was lost**: in a fast-moving market, the delay let a rival act first.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three features of planning.
questions.solution_md: Any three features, each named and explained in a sentence.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Pervasive:** planning is needed at **every level** — the top plans for the whole firm, middle managers for departments and supervisors for daily work.
2. **Futuristic:** it is **forward-looking**, preparing the firm for conditions expected in a coming period.
3. **Involves decision making:** the planner must **choose the best alternative** from several possible courses of action.

questions.stem_md: Before the monsoon, *Arogya Clinic* (an imagined clinic in Kochi) fixes how many fever tests it will stock, assigns each nurse a clear duty and sets a daily target for patients seen. Identify three points of importance of planning reflected here and explain each briefly.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct importance points, each tied to a line of the situation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Provides direction:** each nurse knows her **duty**, so everyone works towards the same goal.
2. **Reduces risks of uncertainty:** stocking tests in advance prepares the clinic for the **expected rise** in fever cases.
3. **Establishes standards for controlling:** the **daily target** lets the clinic compare actual work with the plan.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five points that show the importance of planning for a business.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct importance points, each with a one-line explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Provides direction:** stating goals in advance tells every employee what to work towards.
2. **Reduces risks of uncertainty:** by forecasting changes, managers prepare responses before problems arise.
3. **Reduces overlapping and waste:** coordinated plans prevent duplicate work and idle resources.
4. **Promotes innovative ideas:** searching for the best course of action encourages creative thinking.
5. **Establishes standards for controlling:** planned targets give the yardstick for measuring actual performance.

questions.stem_md: Describe any five features of planning with a short example of each.
questions.solution_md: Five features, each with a brief example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Focuses on objectives:** a bakery plans in order to raise sales, not for its own sake.
2. **Primary function:** staffing and directing follow the plan, so planning comes first.
3. **Pervasive:** a director plans expansion while a supervisor plans the weekly roster.
4. **Continuous:** when a quarterly plan ends, the next quarter's plan is prepared.
5. **Mental exercise:** forecasting next year's demand needs foresight and judgement, not physical work.

questions.stem_md: Planning has several limitations. Explain any five of them.
questions.solution_md: Five limitations, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rigidity:** once fixed, a plan may stop managers from changing course even when a better option appears.
2. **May not work in a dynamic environment:** sudden changes in policy, technology or demand can make a plan useless.
3. **Reduces creativity:** lower-level staff mostly implement plans framed at the top, so their initiative suffers.
4. **Huge costs:** surveys, experts and forecasts make planning expensive.
5. **Time-consuming:** detailed planning may delay action, so opportunities can be lost.

questions.stem_md: Planning is costly, takes time and can make a firm rigid. Yet almost every successful business plans. Evaluate this statement, giving arguments on both sides and your conclusion.
questions.solution_md: Two limitations, two benefits, and a reasoned conclusion that recommends flexible plans with review.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Against:** planning uses money on surveys and experts and takes time, so quick opportunities may be missed.
2. **Against:** a fixed plan can make the firm **rigid** in a changing environment.
3. **For:** planning gives **direction** and helps **anticipate** risks, so the firm is rarely caught unprepared.
4. **For:** it provides **standards for control** and avoids waste.
5. **Conclusion:** the limitations are real but manageable; plans should be **flexible**, reviewed through **follow-up**, so their benefits outweigh their costs.

questions.stem_md: Which is the **first** step in the planning process?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Setting objectives. A firm must first decide what it wants to achieve; premises, alternatives and implementation all follow from the objectives.

questions.stem_md: In the planning process, **premises** are best described as

options.text_md: the buildings and land owned by the business
assumptions about future conditions on which the plan is based
the final targets the business wants to achieve
the rules employees must follow at work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** assumptions about future conditions on which the plan is based. Premises are the forecasts and assumptions (about demand, prices, policy) that form the base of a plan. Business premises in the sense of buildings, objectives and rules are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: The planning team of *Ganga Logistics* (imagined) assumes that diesel prices will rise by about a tenth next year and that a new expressway will open by June. Which step of planning are they at?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Developing premises. Making assumptions about future conditions (fuel prices, a new road) is developing premises. Objectives are goals; selection and follow-up come later.

questions.stem_md: A dairy cooperative compares three ways of reaching city buyers — its own milk booths, supermarkets and a delivery app — by looking at the cost, reach and risk of each. Which step of planning is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Evaluating alternative courses. The options have already been identified; weighing the positives and negatives of each is evaluation. Implementation and premises are different steps.

questions.stem_md: Three months after launching a plan to cut delivery time, the manager of an imagined courier firm checks every week whether the targets are being met and adjusts routes where they are not. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** follow-up action. Monitoring whether a plan is being carried out as intended, and correcting it, is follow-up action, the last step of the process.

questions.stem_md: To raise sales, the owner of an imagined sweet shop in Agra lists the options: open a second outlet, start home delivery, or supply hotels. At this point she has not yet compared them. Which step has she completed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Identifying alternative courses of action. Listing possible courses of action, without comparing them yet, is identifying alternatives. Evaluation and selection come next.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Developing premises is an important step in planning.

**Reason (R):** Plans rest on assumptions about the future, and wrong assumptions can make a plan fail.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since every plan rests on assumptions, they must be developed carefully and shared with all planners.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Planning is a continuous process.

**Reason (R):** Planning involves choosing from among alternative courses of action.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Planning is continuous because one plan is followed by another for the next period; choosing among alternatives explains why planning involves decision making.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Follow-up action is the last step of the planning process.
questions.solution_md: **True.** After the plan is implemented, managers check that it is carried out as intended; this monitoring is the final step.

questions.stem_md: The assumptions about future conditions on which a plan is built are called planning ___.
questions.solution_md: These assumptions are called premises (for example, expected demand, prices or government policy).

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the planning process in the correct order.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (d) → (g) → (c) → (b) → (f) → (e). Goals come first, then assumptions, then the options are listed, weighed and one is chosen; the plan is put into action and finally monitored.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What are planning premises? Give two examples of premises a car-parts maker might use.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of premises plus two suitable forecasts.

answer.model_answer_md: **Premises** are the **assumptions about the future** on which a plan is based. A car-parts maker might assume that (1) **car sales will grow** next year, and (2) **steel prices will stay stable**; its production and purchase plans rest on these forecasts.

questions.stem_md: *Chai Chaupal* (an imagined tea-stall chain in Lucknow) wants to grow. Explain the first three steps of planning it should follow, using its situation as the example.
questions.solution_md: The three steps in order, each applied to the tea-stall chain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Setting objectives:** decide what it wants, e.g. **ten new stalls** within two years.
2. **Developing premises:** assume conditions, e.g. **footfall near colleges** will rise and milk prices stay steady.
3. **Identifying alternatives:** list ways to grow, such as **own stalls, franchises** or a **delivery kitchen**, before comparing them.

questions.stem_md: How is evaluating alternatives different from selecting an alternative? Explain, and say why the manager may choose a combination of courses rather than just one.
questions.solution_md: The difference between the two steps and the reason for choosing a combination.

answer.model_answer_md: **Evaluating** means **weighing the merits and demerits** of each option, e.g. cost, risk and returns. **Selecting** is the **decision** that follows: the best option is **adopted**. A manager may **combine** courses when no single option is best on every count, e.g. using own stores in big cities and dealers in small towns.

questions.stem_md: *Pedal Pathway* (an imagined bicycle maker in Ludhiana) wants to launch electric bicycles. Explain the steps of planning it should follow, using its situation.
questions.solution_md: All seven steps, grouped sensibly, each applied to the e-bike launch.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Objectives:** sell **5,000 e-bikes** in the first year.
2. **Premises:** assume demand from **college students** will grow and battery prices will fall.
3. **Alternatives and evaluation:** list options (make batteries itself, buy them, or partner with a supplier) and compare their cost and risk.
4. **Selection and implementation:** choose the **partnership**, then assign tasks, money and deadlines to departments.
5. **Follow-up:** review **monthly sales** against the target and correct the plan where needed.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **single-use** plan?

options.text_md: A rule that visitors must sign in at the gate
A procedure for approving leave applications
A detailed plan and budget for a company's twenty-fifth anniversary event
A policy of promoting staff from within the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A detailed plan and budget for a company's twenty-fifth anniversary event. An anniversary event happens once, so its plan is single-use. Rules, procedures and policies are used again and again (standing plans).

questions.stem_md: *Annapurna Foods* (imagined) states: "Wherever possible, we buy vegetables from farmer producer organisations within 100 km of our factory." This is an example of a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** policy. It is a general guide to decisions on purchases that still leaves managers judgement ("wherever possible"): a policy. A rule allows no discretion; a procedure is a sequence of steps; a budget is in numbers.

questions.stem_md: A notice at an imagined chemical plant reads: "Safety helmets must be worn on the shop floor at all times. Anyone found without one will be fined ₹500." This is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** rule. It states exactly what must be done, allows no discretion and names a penalty: a rule.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined bank branch, a staff claim for travel expenses is filled in, checked by the branch manager, verified by accounts and then paid. This fixed sequence of steps is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** procedure. A chronological series of steps for a routine activity is a procedure. A method is the way one step is performed.

questions.stem_md: An imagined call centre decides that new staff will be trained by sitting beside experienced colleagues on live calls rather than through classroom lectures. This choice of how a task is done is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** method. A method prescribes the way a particular task (here, training) is to be carried out. A procedure is a sequence of steps; a rule allows no choice; a programme is a detailed plan for a project.

questions.stem_md: *Nirmal Detergents* (imagined) decides to enter rural markets with small low-priced sachets, advertise in regional languages and sell through village shops, putting most of its marketing budget behind this. This is an example of a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** strategy. A comprehensive plan that sets a long-term direction, chooses a course of action and commits resources, in response to the environment, is a strategy.

questions.stem_md: A plan that states expected results in numerical terms for a future period is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** budget. A budget expresses a plan in numbers (rupees, units, hours). It also serves as a control device.

questions.stem_md: "Raise our share of the two-wheeler tyre market in South India from 12 per cent to 15 per cent by March 2028." In the classification of plans, this statement is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an objective. It states an end result to be achieved within a time period: an objective. Rules, procedures and methods concern how work is done.

questions.stem_md: For opening its first store in Guwahati, an imagined furniture retailer prepares a detailed plan listing the tasks, the people responsible, the money needed and the date for each stage. This is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** programme. A detailed statement of a one-time project, covering tasks, resources and timing, is a programme (a single-use plan).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rule leaves no scope for discretion.

**Reason (R):** A rule is a general guide to thinking that allows managers to use their judgement.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: a rule says exactly what must or must not be done. R is false: it describes a policy, not a rule.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A strategy is a comprehensive plan.

**Reason (R):** A strategy covers the long-term direction of the firm, the course of action to reach it and the allocation of resources, keeping the business environment in view.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because a strategy covers direction, action and resources together, it is comprehensive.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A procedure is a single-use plan.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A procedure is a standing plan: the same sequence of steps is used every time the routine activity recurs.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A programme drawn up for launching one new product is a single-use plan.
questions.solution_md: **True.** It covers a one-time project and is not used again once the launch is over, so it is single-use.

questions.stem_md: A statement of expected results expressed in numbers, such as a sales target in units and rupees, is called a ___.
questions.solution_md: Such a numerical plan is a budget.

questions.stem_md: Plans made for a one-time event or project that will not recur are called ___ plans.
questions.solution_md: They are single-use plans, for example a programme or a budget for one event.

questions.stem_md: Match each statement from an imagined pharmacy chain with the type of plan it represents.

options.text_md: "We try to stock generic medicines wherever a doctor permits it."
"No medicine may be sold after its expiry date."
"Receive the order, check the batch number, enter it in the register, shelve it."
"Count stock by scanning barcodes, not by hand."

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). A guide with room for judgement is a policy; a strict do or do not is a rule; a sequence of steps is a procedure; the way one task is done is a method.

questions.stem_md: *Steamwell Appliances* (imagined) plans to sell 12,000 pressure cookers next year at ₹1,250 each. What is the value of its sales budget in rupees?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sales budget = units × price.
Step 2: 12,000 × 1,250 = 1,50,00,000. So ₹1,50,00,000.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a policy and a rule on any two bases.
questions.solution_md: Two bases, each stating the position of both a policy and a rule.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Discretion:** a **policy** is a general guide that **allows judgement**; a **rule** allows **no discretion**.
2. **Penalty:** breaking a rule usually carries a **penalty**; a policy only guides decisions and has no fixed penalty.

questions.stem_md: How is a method different from a procedure? Explain with one example from a school office.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of each and an example that shows the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: A **procedure** is the **sequence of steps** for a routine job; a **method** is the **way one step is done**. Fee collection in a school office follows a procedure (receive, record, issue receipt); recording the fee **on a computer instead of a ledger** is a method.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between single-use and standing plans, giving one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Both types defined with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Single-use plans** are made for a **one-time** event and lapse after it, e.g. a **budget for an annual sports day**. **Standing plans** are used **repeatedly** for recurring situations, e.g. a **policy** of promoting staff from within.

questions.stem_md: What is a strategy? Explain the three things a strategy decides, using an imagined bakery chain planning to expand into a new state.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the three dimensions, each applied to the bakery.

answer.model_answer_md:
A **strategy** is a **comprehensive plan** for reaching long-term goals in the light of the environment. It decides:
1. **Long-term objectives:** e.g. **thirty outlets** in Telangana in five years.
2. **Course of action:** e.g. local flavours and **franchise** outlets.
3. **Allocation of resources:** e.g. most of the **expansion fund** to the first ten outlets.

questions.stem_md: Explain objectives as a type of plan. Rewrite the vague goal "We want to do better in exports" as a useful objective, and state two qualities your version has.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of objectives, a rewritten objective and two qualities it has.

answer.model_answer_md: **Objectives** are the **end results** an organisation aims to achieve; all other plans serve them. A useful version: "**Raise export sales by 20 per cent by March 2028.**" It is (1) **measurable**, because results can be checked in numbers, and (2) **time-bound**, because it states a deadline.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five types of plans, with one example of each from an imagined hospital.
questions.solution_md: Five types, each with a meaning and a hospital example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Objective:** the end result, e.g. cut patient waiting time to **twenty minutes** by next year.
2. **Policy:** a general guide, e.g. **emergency cases are treated first**, whatever the queue.
3. **Procedure:** steps in sequence, e.g. register the patient, record vital signs, then send to the doctor.
4. **Rule:** no discretion, e.g. **no visitors in the intensive care unit**.
5. **Budget:** a plan in numbers, e.g. **₹40 lakh** for new equipment this year.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage about Vegam Motors and answer the questions on the planning process that follow. *(Imagined company, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Assumptions about the future are premises.

**(b)** The line that lists the options before they are compared.

**(c) (i)** After selection come implementation and follow-up.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two sound reasons for combining courses of action.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Developing premises.**

**(b)** The line beginning "**Next, the team listed three ways to sell...**", which names showrooms, dealers and online selling.

**(c) (i)** 1. **Implementing the plan:** assign dealers, staff, money and deadlines so that the chosen mix is put into action.
2. **Follow-up action:** regularly compare actual scooter sales with the 20,000 target and correct the plan if needed.

**OR (c) (ii)** 1. **No single option is best everywhere:** dealers suit big cities with many buyers, while online sales reach small towns cheaply.
2. **Spreading risk:** using two channels means a problem with one does not stop all sales.

questions.passage_md:
**Vegam Motors, Coimbatore (imagined)**

The board of Vegam Motors decided to sell 20,000 electric scooters in Tamil Nadu within two years. The planning team then worked on the assumption that state support for electric vehicles would continue and that battery prices would keep falling. Next, the team listed three ways to sell: opening company showrooms, appointing dealers, or selling only online. Each option was studied for its cost, speed and risk. The team chose to appoint dealers in big cities and sell online in smaller towns.

children.stem_md: Identify the step of planning shown by: "...worked on the assumption that state support for electric vehicles would continue..."
children.solution_md: Assumptions about the future are premises.

answer.model_answer_md: **Developing premises.**

children.stem_md: Quote the line that shows the step "identifying alternative courses of action".
children.solution_md: The line that lists the options before they are compared.

answer.model_answer_md: The line beginning "**Next, the team listed three ways to sell...**", which names showrooms, dealers and online selling.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Name and explain the two steps of planning that Vegam Motors still has to carry out.
children.solution_md: After selection come implementation and follow-up.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Implementing the plan:** assign dealers, staff, money and deadlines so that the chosen mix is put into action.
2. **Follow-up action:** regularly compare actual scooter sales with the 20,000 target and correct the plan if needed.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why might the team have chosen a combination of dealers and online sales rather than a single option? Give two reasons.
alternatives.solution_md: Two sound reasons for combining courses of action.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No single option is best everywhere:** dealers suit big cities with many buyers, while online sales reach small towns cheaply.
2. **Spreading risk:** using two channels means a problem with one does not stop all sales.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from the Neelgiri Garments handbook and answer the questions on types of plans that follow. *(Imagined firm, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** A general guide that leaves room for judgement ("unless supplies are short") is a policy.

**(b)** Expected sales in units and rupees for a future period make it a budget.

**(c) (i)** Name both plans and give a valid difference.

**OR (c) (ii)** Classify all four statements and give the reason for each group.
